product.name: HARNESSED
product.tagline: From zero to a hireable AI harness engineer, one replayable run at a time.
product.mnemonic: Clever Crews Launch Early; Test Pilots Verify Often.

wires.name: Control plane
wires.question: What is the model told, and which instruction wins?

wires.name: Context & memory
wires.question: What is on the desk this call, and what is saved?

wires.name: Loop & state
wires.question: What happens next, what do we carry, when do we stop?
wires.law: Every run needs more than one exit.

wires.name: Errors & recovery
wires.question: When something fails, how do we continue without spinning?

wires.name: Tools
wires.question: What can the model do, and is each tool easy to use?
wires.law: A tool is a user interface for a model.

wires.name: Permissions & sandbox
wires.question: Which actions are allowed, and how bad can a mistake get?
wires.law: Judge the action and its target.

wires.name: Verification & evals
wires.question: How do we know it's really done, and did the change help?

wires.name: Observability
wires.question: What exactly happened, and where did time and money go?
wires.law: If it isn't in the trace, it didn't happen.

failure_families.name: False “done”
failure_families.summary: The agent reports success it never checked.

failure_families.name: The confident lie
failure_families.summary: Fluent, specific, wrong: an invented function, flag or fact.

failure_families.name: The forgetful harness
failure_families.summary: History isn't resent, so the model starts from nothing.

failure_families.name: First block only
failure_families.summary: Code reads only content[0] and misses or crashes on other blocks.

failure_families.name: Schema drift
failure_families.summary: Model output has the wrong shape and breaks code downstream.

failure_families.name: Effort mismatch
failure_families.summary: Maximum reasoning on easy work: same answers, many times the cost and wait.

failure_families.name: Long-chain collapse
failure_families.summary: Small per-step error rates multiply until long tasks mostly fail.

failure_families.name: Split tool results
failure_families.summary: Parallel results sent in separate messages or with mismatched ids.

failure_families.name: The “almost done” spiral
failure_families.summary: A loop with one exit keeps calling tools forever.

failure_families.name: Harness regression
failure_families.summary: A harness change, not the model, quietly makes results worse.

failure_families.name: The ignored rule
failure_families.summary: A prompt-only rule holds early and breaks late in a long run.

failure_families.name: Context flood
failure_families.summary: One giant tool output buries the task.

failure_families.name: Compaction amnesia
failure_families.summary: A summary drops a constraint or redoes finished work.

failure_families.name: Cold cache
failure_families.summary: A changing prefix (a timestamp, reordered tools) defeats prompt caching.

failure_families.name: Orphaned tool call
failure_families.summary: An interrupt leaves a tool_use with no tool_result, and resume fails.

failure_families.name: Retry storm
failure_families.summary: Clients retry in lockstep without jitter and prolong the outage.

failure_families.name: Tool confusion
failure_families.summary: A vague name or schema makes the model call the wrong tool or wrong inputs.

failure_families.name: Tool overload
failure_families.summary: Too many tool definitions eat the window and blur the choice.

failure_families.name: Approval fatigue
failure_families.summary: So many prompts that the dangerous one gets approved too.

failure_families.name: Sandbox escape
failure_families.summary: A symlink or ../ path reaches outside the workspace.

failure_families.name: Reviewer rubber-stamp
failure_families.summary: A reviewer or judge that shares the author's view approves everything.

failure_families.name: The unexplained bill
failure_families.summary: Cost jumps and nobody can say where it went.

failure_families.name: Secret in the trace
failure_families.summary: A key or token is written into logs that many people can read.

failure_families.name: Works on my examples
failure_families.summary: A change looks fine on three examples and breaks many real tasks.

failure_families.name: Noise mistaken for progress
failure_families.summary: A difference that is inside the noise is reported as an improvement.

failure_families.name: The injected page
failure_families.summary: Instructions hidden in fetched content steer the agent.

failure_families.name: The poisoned tool
failure_families.summary: A tool's description or server is malicious or compromised.

failure_families.name: Sub-agent sprawl
failure_families.summary: Many agents, many times the cost, conflicting work.

failure_families.name: Shift amnesia
failure_families.summary: A new session redoes or undoes the last one's work.

failure_families.name: The lost session
failure_families.summary: The process dies and the run's state dies with it.

failure_families.name: The cheap-model trap
failure_families.summary: Cheaper per call, more expensive per completed task.

failure_families.name: Double charge
failure_families.summary: A retried action with side effects runs twice.

failure_families.name: Reward hack
failure_families.summary: The policy satisfies the grader instead of the task.

failure_families.name: Migration break
failure_families.summary: A new model rejects or changes something the harness relied on.

failure_families.name: The stale map
failure_families.summary: Agents follow outdated rules or docs as the codebase drifts.

modules.title: Same model, different harness
modules.law: Same model, different harness, different results.

objectives.text: Replay an agent run and describe it as a sequence of model calls and tool actions.
Predict whether a run's “done” is real before replaying it, then check your prediction.
Change one harness setting and measure its effect over 20 seeded trials as a pass rate.
State the course thesis with your own numbers: same model, different harness, different results.
Find your way around the course: the five beats, the eight wires, your Harness Board, and progress export.

misconceptions: “A better model is the only way to get better results.”
“If the agent says it's done, it's done.”
“One good run proves the setup works.”

modules.title: What a model does
modules.law: A model predicts; it doesn't know.

objectives.text: Explain next-token prediction: the model scores every possible next token and a sampler picks one.
Predict how temperature changes the spread of outputs, then check it in the Sampler.
Explain why a fluent, confident answer can be false, and why fluency is not evidence.
Distinguish training from inference, and say which one a harness engineer controls.

misconceptions: “Temperature 0 makes the model correct and repeatable.”
“The model learns from our conversation as we talk.”

modules.title: Tokens and the context window
modules.law: Everything on the desk costs tokens.

objectives.text: Estimate the token count of a text with the course's rule of thumb, then check it in the Tokenizer.
Explain the context window as one fixed-size desk shared by instructions, history, tool results and the reply.
Distinguish the input limit from the output limit, and predict what happens when each is hit.
Explain why tokens drive cost and latency.

misconceptions: “The context window is memory that lasts between chats.”
“If it fits in the window, the model reads all of it equally well.”

modules.title: The stateless model
modules.law: The messages array is the memory.

objectives.text: Explain why each model call starts from nothing, and where conversation memory actually lives.
Build a conversation by appending user and assistant messages and resending the whole list.
Predict what the model can know on a given call from the list that was sent.
Name three kinds of memory (in the window, in saved files, in the weights) and say which the harness controls.

misconceptions: “The API keeps the conversation for me.”

modules.title: The API call on the wire
modules.law: Read the whole reply: every block, every stop reason.

objectives.text: Read a Messages API request and response in the Wire View and name each part.
Explain why a reply is a list of typed content blocks, not one string.
Handle every stop_reason value the API can return, on purpose.
Read the usage fields to get a call's input and output tokens and its cost.
Describe streaming as a sequence of events that build the same message.

misconceptions: “The first content block is the answer.”
“stop_reason only matters when something goes wrong.”

modules.title: Structured outputs and schemas
modules.law: Valid isn't true: check the shape, then the meaning.

objectives.text: Write a JSON Schema for a small object using types, required fields, enums and additionalProperties.
Validate model output against a schema and turn a validation error into a message the model can fix.
Compare three ways to get structured output: asking in the prompt, validating afterwards, and constrained decoding.
Say what a strict schema guarantees and what it cannot (the values can still be wrong).

misconceptions: “A schema in the prompt guarantees the shape.”
“If parsing fails, the harness should crash.”

modules.title: Reasoning and effort as harness knobs
modules.law: Effort is a dial with a price.

objectives.text: Explain extended thinking: extra tokens the model writes before answering, billed as output.
Predict how raising effort changes pass rate, cost and latency on easy and hard tasks, then measure it on the Bench.
Explain why thinking blocks must be passed back unchanged during a tool loop.
Choose an effort level for a class of tasks and justify it with cost per completed task.

misconceptions: “The visible thinking is a faithful record of why the model acted.”

modules.title: Why a model alone is unreliable
modules.law: Small errors multiply; the harness has to catch them.

objectives.text: Name the six weaknesses of a model alone (hallucination, randomness, drift, self-praise, no ground truth, stale knowledge) and give an example of each.
Compute how per-step reliability compounds over n steps, and predict the success of a 30-step task at 98 % per step.
Explain the first principle: reliability comes from the system around the model, checked from outside.
Argue both sides of “models keep getting better, so harnesses matter less”, with evidence.

misconceptions: “A model that is right 98 % of the time is reliable enough for long tasks.”
“Next year's model will make the harness unnecessary.”

modules.title: Tools give the model hands
modules.law: The model asks; the harness acts.

objectives.text: Explain the trick: the model only writes a tool request, and the harness runs it and sends back the result.
Write a tool definition with a name, a description and an input schema.
Match every tool_result to its tool_use id, mark failures with is_error, and return all results for one turn in a single user message.
Explain why a tool is a user interface for a model.

misconceptions: “A tool error should crash the harness.”
“Each tool result goes in its own message.”

modules.title: The agent loop
modules.law: Every run needs more than one exit.

objectives.text: Write the agent loop: call the model, run the requested tools, append the results, and repeat until it stops asking.
Handle each stop_reason on purpose: tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens, and the rest.
Explain why a single exit is not enough, and add a turn limit and a token budget.
Read a replay of a loop and say, for any event, which turn it belongs to and what the loop does next.
Point to where each of the other seven wires plugs into the loop.

misconceptions: “The model decides when to stop, so it will stop.”
“The loop is a framework detail I don't need to understand.”

modules.title: What a harness is
modules.law: Agent = Model + Harness.

objectives.text: Use Agent = Model + Harness to sort behaviors into “the model” or “the harness”.
Distinguish prompt engineering, context engineering and harness engineering.
Explain the operating-system picture of an agent and where the picture breaks down.
Distinguish the product harness a vendor ships from the user harness you add around it.
Cite evidence that harness changes alone move results, and one counterpoint.

misconceptions: “The harness is just the system prompt.”
“Frameworks and harnesses are the same thing.”
“If results got worse, the model got worse.”

modules.title: The Turn Clock
modules.law: One turn, eight wires, one order.

objectives.text: Name the eight wires in turn order and the question each one answers.
Walk one turn around the clock out loud, saying what each wire does.
Name the wire at fault for a failure shown in a replay.
Match each wire to its law.

misconceptions: “The wires are separate features you add one by one.”

modules.title: Control plane: instructions as law
modules.law: Words guide, code enforces.

objectives.text: Assemble a prompt from layers and predict which instruction wins when two conflict.
Write an instruction at the right altitude: specific enough to act on, general enough to transfer.
Move a rule that matters from the prompt into code with a pre-tool hook that fails closed, and show it holds.
Structure a project rules file (AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) as a map, not a manual.
Treat prompt lines as code: version them, review them and test them.

misconceptions: “Writing MUST or NEVER makes a rule enforced.”

modules.title: Context budget
modules.law: The smallest window that works.

objectives.text: Explain context rot: answer quality falls as the window fills, well before the hard limit.
Audit a trace to find what eats the budget: instructions, tool definitions, history or tool outputs.
Apply the four levers in order: don't load it, shrink it, move it out, summarize it.
Cap a tool's output so it points to more instead of dumping everything.
Order context for attention: stable material first, the current task last.

misconceptions: “The model reads the whole window equally well.”

modules.title: Compaction and memory
modules.law: Summarize the story, keep the commitments.

objectives.text: Explain compaction and its main failure: losing what matters.
Write a compactor that keeps the goal, constraints, decisions, progress and file pointers, and drops raw tool output.
Choose between compaction and a clean reset with a handoff note, and give reasons.
Describe the memory tiers (window, session log, project files, long-term store) and what belongs in each.

modules.title: Prompt caching
modules.law: Stable first, changing last.

objectives.text: Explain prompt caching as exact prefix matching: one changed byte invalidates everything after it.
Order a request (tools, system, stable context, history, new turn) to maximize cache hits.
Find a silent cache invalidator in a Wire View diff.
Compute the cache hit rate and the savings from a response's usage fields.

misconceptions: “A small change only invalidates the changed part.”

modules.title: Loop state and stopping well
modules.law: Close the books before you stop.

objectives.text: Keep all run state in one state object and change it in one place.
Give every way a run can end its own exit and final status.
Handle an interrupt so that no tool call is left without a result.
Pause and resume a run from saved state, keeping history append-only.
Detect a loop (the same action again and again) and stop it.

misconceptions: “After an interrupt, just retry from scratch.”

modules.title: Errors are the main path
modules.law: Errors are the main path.

objectives.text: Classify an error as transient, permanent or the model's mistake, and route each one correctly.
Write retries with exponential backoff, jitter and a cap, and explain why jitter matters.
Add a circuit breaker and a retry budget so recovery has brakes of its own.
Keep wrong outputs and error messages in context so the model can correct itself.
Make a retried action safe with an idempotency key.

modules.title: Tool design is agent UX
modules.law: A tool is a user interface for a model.

objectives.text: Apply the six rules for tools that work to a weak tool and fix it.
Write descriptions and schemas that make wrong calls hard: clear names, enums, required fields and examples.
Return results and errors that tell the model what to do next, in few tokens.
Describe a tool's risk with annotations: read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world.
Batch tool calls into rounds that are safe to run in parallel.

misconceptions: “More tools make the agent more capable.”

modules.title: MCP, skills and tool scale
modules.law: Load the menu, not the kitchen.

objectives.text: Describe MCP's shape: hosts and clients, servers, transports, and the primitives a server offers.
Explain skills: a short description loaded up front, the full procedure loaded only when needed.
Measure what many tool definitions cost in tokens and accuracy, then apply tool search or deferred loading.
Explain how letting the model write code that calls tools can replace many tool round trips.
Vet an MCP server before connecting it: who wrote it, what it can reach, how it is pinned.

modules.title: Permissions
modules.law: Judge the action and its target.

objectives.text: Return allow, ask or deny for each tool call, always with a reason.
Judge risk as action × target: the same command can be safe in one place and dangerous in another.
Explain approval fatigue and write rules that ask rarely, and only when it matters.
Apply a fixed decision order: deny rules, then ask rules, then allow rules, then the mode's default.
Write a permission policy as code and test it with a table of cases.

modules.title: Sandboxes: blast walls
modules.law: Assume the wall will be tested.

objectives.text: Explain a sandbox as a blast wall that limits how bad a mistake can get, whatever the permissions said.
Confine file access to a workspace root and defeat path traversal and symlinks.
Restrict network egress with an allow-list, and explain why exfiltration needs the network.
Keep secrets out of the sandbox and out of the trace.
Compare OS sandboxes, containers and virtual machines by isolation, speed and cost.

misconceptions: “A string prefix check on paths is enough.”

modules.title: Verification: done is a claim
modules.law: “Done” is a claim.

objectives.text: Put a verification gate between the model's done claim and the run's success.
Prefer computational checks (tests, linters, type checks) over inferential ones, and say when each fits.
Distinguish guides, which steer before the work, from sensors, which check after it.
Set up an independent reviewer that sees the task and the diff, not the author's reasoning.
Spot and block test tampering: edited tests, special-cased answers, skipped checks.

misconceptions: “The agent said the tests pass, so they pass.”
“A reviewer model with the same context is independent.”
“More checks always make the run slower.”

modules.title: Observability: traces you can read
modules.law: If it isn't in the trace, it didn't happen.

objectives.text: Record the events that matter, with ids, timing, tokens and cost.
Read a trace and find the first event where things went wrong.
Structure a trace as spans (run, turn, model call, tool call) and map them to the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.
Redact secrets before they reach the trace.
Answer “where did the time and money go?” from a trace.

modules.title: Eval anatomy
modules.law: No number, no claim.

objectives.text: Name the parts of an eval: task, environment, trials, grader, transcript and outcome.
Choose a grader (code, model or human) for a task and name how each can fail.
Write a small eval with a code grader and run it over seeded trials.
Distinguish capability evals from regression evals.

misconceptions: “A few hand-picked examples are an eval.”
“Evals are for model makers, not harness engineers.”

modules.title: Statistics for a random system
modules.law: One run is an anecdote.

objectives.text: Compute pass@k and pass^k from trial results and explain why they tell opposite stories.
Compute a 95 % confidence interval for a pass rate and judge whether two results really differ.
Estimate how many trials you need to detect a given difference.
Name sources of noise beyond sampling: infrastructure, time limits and flaky checks.

misconceptions: “A higher number on 10 trials is an improvement.”
“pass@k and pass^k measure the same thing.”
“The model is the only source of randomness.”

modules.title: Evals in practice
modules.law: Grade the grader.

objectives.text: Run regression evals in CI and block a change that falls below a noise-aware threshold.
Calibrate a model grader against human labels and report how often they agree.
Explain contamination and models that notice they are being tested, and reduce their effect.
Read eval transcripts to find graders that pass work for the wrong reason.

misconceptions: “A public benchmark measures my use case.”
“Once an eval is written, it stays valid.”

modules.title: Prompt injection and the lethal trifecta
modules.law: Remove a leg; don't ask nicely.

objectives.text: Explain prompt injection: instructions hidden in content the agent reads.
Find the three legs of the lethal trifecta in a tool set: private data, untrusted content, and a way to send data out.
Remove one leg by design and show the attack fails, where prompt wording only lowers the rate.
Explain why “the model will ignore malicious text” is not a defense.

misconceptions: “Only web pages carry injections; tool output is safe.”

modules.title: Defense in layers
modules.law: Every layer fails sometimes; stack them.

objectives.text: Layer defenses (least privilege, sandbox, egress control, confirmation, monitoring) and say what each one stops.
Audit a tool supply chain: pin, review and isolate MCP servers, and spot tool poisoning.
Remove excessive agency by applying least privilege to a tool set.
Red-team your own agent with a seeded attack suite and report the attack success rate.

modules.title: Many agents: when and how
modules.law: Add agents for a reason, not for a picture.

objectives.text: Name the two honest reasons for many agents (parallel work, context isolation) and the warning that comes with them.
Compare five topologies by cost, wall-clock time and failure modes.
Choose an isolated or a forked context for a sub-agent and explain the trade-off.
Write a sub-agent brief whose result can be checked.
Treat a multi-agent system as a distributed system: timeouts, partial failure, conflicting writes, cleanup.

misconceptions: “A sub-agent's output is as trustworthy as your own code.”

modules.title: Long-running agents
modules.law: Leave the desk ready for the next shift.

objectives.text: Explain the shift-worker problem: each new session starts with no memory of the last one.
Use the initializer pattern: a first session that sets up the environment, a feature list and a progress file.
Split work into planner, generator and evaluator roles with clear handoffs.
Write a handoff note the next session can act on without guessing.

misconceptions: “The next session will figure it out from the code.”
“The agent can grade its own long task.”

modules.title: Managed agents: the harness as a service
modules.law: Keep the state outside the process.

objectives.text: Describe a managed agent as a brain (model and loop), hands (sandboxes and tools) and a session (an append-only event log).
Explain how separating the three lets each one fail and be replaced alone.
Explain why credentials stay with the brain, outside the sandbox.
Decide when a managed agent service fits better than your own harness, and when it doesn't.

misconceptions: “The session log is the context window.”
“Managed means I don't need to understand the harness.”

modules.title: Cost and latency engineering
modules.law: Price the outcome, not the call.

objectives.text: Compute cost per completed task from trial results, not cost per call.
Cut cost with caching, batching, effort and model routing, and predict each one's effect before measuring.
Set budgets per run and per task, and degrade gracefully when one is hit.
Find the main sources of latency in a trace and reduce them.

misconceptions: “The cheapest model is the cheapest option.”

modules.title: Production: agents that survive real traffic
modules.law: Assume the process dies mid-step.

objectives.text: Handle rate limits with a queue and a token bucket, and honor retry-after.
Make runs durable: checkpoint after each step and resume without repeating side effects.
Design streaming and human-in-the-loop screens that show progress and ask clearly.
Roll out a harness change gradually (shadow, canary, A/B) with eval gates.

misconceptions: “It works on my laptop, so it works.”
“Ship the new harness to everyone at once if evals pass.”

modules.title: Environments: harnesses that train and test models
modules.law: The grader is the spec.

objectives.text: Describe an environment: tasks, a sandbox, tools, a grader and a reward.
Make an environment deterministic and resettable so results can be reproduced.
Find a reward hack that a scripted policy exploits, and close it in the grader.
Explain how eval environments and training environments differ in what they need.
Contain an environment: no network egress by default, scoped credentials, and monitoring for unexpected actions.

misconceptions: “A passing grader means a solved task.”

modules.title: Model migrations: when the model changes under you
modules.law: New model, old assumptions: test them again.

objectives.text: Read a model migration guide and list the changes that break your harness: removed parameters, new stop reasons, changed defaults.
Put model-specific behavior behind one adapter with capability checks, so a migration is a config change plus a test run.
Run a regression eval on the old and the new model and decide with intervals, not impressions.
Retire harness parts the new model no longer needs and keep the ones it still does, with evidence for each.

misconceptions: “A newer model is a drop-in replacement.”
“If the API call succeeds, nothing broke.”
“Prompts tuned for one model transfer unchanged.”

modules.title: Inside Claude Code, wire by wire
modules.law: Read real harnesses wire by wire.

objectives.text: Map Claude Code's main features onto the eight wires.
Explain four design lessons worth stealing from it.
Read a vendor postmortem and name the wire and failure family behind each issue.

misconceptions: “A product harness is a black box I can't learn from.”

modules.title: Codex and open harnesses: what everyone agrees on
modules.law: Laws are what everyone agrees on; the rest is taste.

objectives.text: Compare Codex and Claude Code wire by wire, naming each design choice and its trade-off.
Explain what OpenAI's harness engineering report found, labeled as the company's own numbers.
Name the ideas every serious harness shares and where they differ.

modules.title: Reading a real harness repository
modules.law: Find the loop first.

objectives.text: Read an unfamiliar harness in a set order: the loop, the model adapter, tools, config, then the trace.
Locate each of the eight wires in a real repository, or note that it is missing.
Run the harness locally on a toy task (with its test model or your own key) and read its trajectory.
Propose one change and say how you would measure it.

modules.title: The daily craft
modules.law: Name the failure before you fix it.

objectives.text: Run the steering loop: watch, name the failure family, fix the harness, measure.
Name the failure family of an incident before choosing a fix.
Build to delete: prefer harness parts that can be removed when models improve, and spot ones that should go.
Fight entropy on a schedule with mechanical checks and cleanup agents.
Make a codebase easy to harness: fast checks, clear errors, readable structure, docs as a map.

modules.title: Rein setup
modules.law: Script first, then go live.

objectives.text: Run Rein in the browser with the scripted model.
Set up a local Python environment and run Rein offline with a scenario tape.
Explain why the build starts with a scripted model: repeatable, free and offline.
Configure a real model with your own API key, kept out of the browser and out of git (optional).

misconceptions: “I need an API key to start.”
“A scripted model teaches nothing about real models.”

modules.title: Rein 1: talk to a model
modules.law: One interface, many models.

objectives.text: Define one model interface with a scripted and a real implementation behind it.
Print a reply with its stop_reason and token usage.
Show statelessness: three separate runs of one script don't remember each other.

misconceptions: “The fake and real models need different code paths.”

modules.title: Rein 2: one tool and the loop
modules.law: The model asks; the harness acts.

objectives.text: Add a tool registry and run the tool calls the model requests.
Implement the agent loop with a turn limit.
Return tool errors to the model as is_error results instead of crashing.

misconceptions: “An unknown tool name should raise an exception.”

modules.title: Rein 3: real tools inside a wall
modules.law: Assume the wall will be tested.

objectives.text: Add file and shell tools that only work inside a workspace root.
Cap every tool's output.
Defeat path traversal in your own tool code and prove it with a hostile tape.

misconceptions: “Running in a practice folder is enough isolation.”

modules.title: Rein 4: the permission gate
modules.law: Judge the action and its target.

objectives.text: Add a gate that returns allow, ask or deny with a reason before any tool runs.
Apply the decision order and test the policy with a table of cases.
Show the gate stopping a dangerous call that the model asked for politely.

misconceptions: “The gate can be added after the tools are written.”

modules.title: Rein 5: a trace
modules.law: If it isn't in the trace, it didn't happen.

objectives.text: Write every harness event to a JSONL trace with the course's event schema.
Load your own trace into the Replay Deck and read it.
Keep the trace useful: ids, turns, tokens, and no secrets.

modules.title: Rein 6: a context budget
modules.law: The smallest window that works.

objectives.text: Estimate the tokens of every request before sending it.
Cap and trim to stay inside a budget, and record what was dropped in the trace.
Show the flood tape passing with the budget and failing without it.

misconceptions: “The provider will reject it if it's too big, so I don't need a budget.”

modules.title: Rein 7: retries and a breaker
modules.law: Errors are the main path.

objectives.text: Retry transient model errors with backoff and jitter on a virtual clock.
Open a circuit breaker after repeated failures and end the run with a clear status.
Show the outage tape: a calm breaker instead of a retry storm.

modules.title: Rein 8: guards that stop the run well
modules.law: Every run needs more than one exit.

objectives.text: Add guards for turns, tokens, time and repeated actions, each with its own final status.
Close the books on interrupt: every pending tool call gets a result.
Show each guard firing on its own tape.

misconceptions: “A turn limit is the only guard I need.”

modules.title: Rein 9: the verification gate
modules.law: “Done” is a claim.

objectives.text: Run the project's checks when the model claims done.
Send failures back to the model, and end with status unverified when checks can't pass.
Show the false-done tape caught by the gate.

misconceptions: “If the model ran the tests itself, I don't need to.”

modules.title: Rein 10: project rules
modules.law: Words guide, code enforces.

objectives.text: Load project rules from a file into the right layer of the prompt.
Enforce one rule in code with a hook, and show the difference against the prompt-only version.
Keep the stable prefix stable so the prompt stays cacheable.

misconceptions: “Rules belong in the system prompt only.”

modules.title: Rein 11: a reviewer sub-agent
modules.law: Independence is designed, not assumed.

objectives.text: Start a reviewer sub-agent with its own fresh context and a narrow brief.
Give it only what independence needs: the task, the diff and the check output.
Show the reviewer catching what the tests missed, and measure how often it rubber-stamps.

misconceptions: “Any second model call is an independent review.”

modules.title: From one file to a project
modules.law: Ship the numbers with the code.

objectives.text: Turn the build's checkpoints into an automated test suite.
Package Rein as a small project with typed code, tests and an eval runner.
Run a real eval with a real model on a small capped budget and record the numbers with intervals.
Run your first experiment: one harness change, measured against a baseline.
Write a showcase README a reviewer can verify.

misconceptions: “One good real run proves the harness works.”

modules.title: Rein extensions, ranked
modules.law: Extend where the evidence points.

objectives.text: Pick an extension by expected learning and hiring value, not by novelty.
Scope it with a measurable success criterion before writing code.
Report the result honestly, including a null result.

misconceptions: “The most impressive extension is the best one.”

modules.title: The job map
modules.law: Evidence beats adjectives.

objectives.text: Name the roles that hire harness engineers and what each does day to day.
Map a job posting's requirements to the eight wires and to evidence you can show.
Explain what AI labs look for in this work: building, measuring and debugging, shown in public.

misconceptions: “The title matters more than the work.”

modules.title: Readiness self-assessment
modules.law: Claim only what you can show.

objectives.text: Read your readiness radar and name the evidence behind each level.
Adjust a level honestly and pick your two weakest wires to work on next.
Produce a brag sheet in which every claim links to evidence.

modules.title: Four portfolio projects
modules.law: A result is a number, an interval and a method.

objectives.text: Choose one of four portfolio projects and scope it to two weeks.
Fill a results table with real numbers and confidence intervals.
Write a technical write-up that a reviewer can reproduce.

modules.title: Capstone: Rein in Rust
modules.law: Same spec, same traces, any language.

objectives.text: Implement the course's engine spec in Rust as a third runtime, with the same tapes, boards and command line as the JS simulator and Rein.
Prove the port with golden-trace parity: byte-identical events and matching wire digests on every seed tape.
Explain where languages drift apart (integer math, JSON key order, string escaping, random numbers) and how one exact spec keeps three runtimes in step.
Present the capstone in an interview: the design, the parity evidence and one bug that parity caught.

misconceptions: “If the port passes the examples, it behaves the same.”

modules.title: Interview Room
modules.law: Walk the clock out loud.

objectives.text: Answer interview questions out loud and self-grade against a rubric.
Solve timed coding katas from memory.
Run a system design answer with the eight-wire checklist, including cost, risks and rollout.
Debug a failing trace under time pressure.
Tell two behavioral stories with evidence.

modules.title: Twelve weeks after the course
modules.law: Practice in public, on a schedule.

objectives.text: Plan twelve weeks of practice with weekly evidence goals.
Run a mock interview with a friend using the kit.
Keep your board energized with the daily shift.

modules.title: Python typing and dataclasses
modules.law: Types are documentation the checker reads.

objectives.text: Annotate functions and variables with types, including optional and union types.
Define a dataclass with defaults and use it as a record.
Run mypy and fix a type error it reports.

modules.title: asyncio
modules.law: Await what waits; don't block the loop.

objectives.text: Write and run coroutines with async and await.
Run independent waits concurrently with gather and a timeout.
Spot code that blocks the event loop.

modules.title: subprocess and signals
modules.law: Every child process needs a timeout.

objectives.text: Run a command with subprocess, capturing output and the exit code.
Add a timeout and handle it.
Explain what SIGINT and SIGTERM do to a running child.

modules.title: JSON Schema in depth
modules.law: Say what's allowed, not just what's expected.

objectives.text: Write schemas with nested objects, arrays and enums.
Use required and additionalProperties to reject unexpected input.
Validate data with the jsonschema library and read its errors.

misconceptions: “A schema without required fields requires them.”

modules.title: HTTP and SSE streaming
modules.law: A stream is a message in pieces.

objectives.text: Read an HTTP request and response: method, headers, status, body.
Explain status codes that matter to agents: 400, 401, 429, 500, 529.
Parse a server-sent events stream into events.

misconceptions: “A 200 status means the whole stream succeeded.”

modules.title: pytest
modules.law: A test that can't fail proves nothing.

objectives.text: Write test functions with plain asserts and run them.
Use fixtures and parametrize to cover many cases.
Check that a test fails on purpose before trusting it.

modules.title: Containers
modules.law: A container is a process with a smaller view.

objectives.text: Explain what a container isolates and what it shares with the host.
Run a command in a container with no network and a read-only filesystem.
Mount only the folder a task needs.

modules.title: git for agent work
modules.law: Commits are the undo button.

objectives.text: Make small commits and read a diff.
Undo an agent's change safely with restore and revert.
Use a branch or worktree to isolate an agent's work.

modules.title: Linux processes
modules.law: Know who your process is and what it can touch.

objectives.text: Read a process's id, parent, user and working directory.
Explain file permissions and why the agent's user matters.
Find and stop a runaway child process.

modules.title: Threads vs. async
modules.law: Concurrency is about waiting, not speed.

objectives.text: Choose threads, async or processes for a given kind of work.
Run parallel-safe tool calls concurrently and collect results in order.
Explain a race condition on a shared file.

misconceptions: “Threads make Python code run in parallel.”
